biography: Peter Faber belonged to the first companions of Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier in Paris. As a priest, he celebrated the Mass at Montmartre in 1534 during which the companions made their commitments. That group became the nucleus of the Society of Jesus.

When Ignatius left Paris in 1535, Faber cared for the companions and helped their community grow. He guided Claude le Jay, Jean Codure, and Paschase Broët through conversation and the Spiritual Exercises. His contribution to the emerging order included sustaining friendships as well as welcoming new members.

His later work took him through a Europe divided by religious conflict. The Society of Jesus's account describes his efforts toward understanding at Worms and Ratisbon, alongside teaching and preaching. His Memorial records an inner life of prayer that accompanied these journeys. He died in Rome in 1546, shortly after arriving exhausted from Coimbra.

In a 2014 homily, Pope Francis presented Faber's gentleness and ability to form friendships as central to his ministry. Francis connected Faber's prayer with his willingness to travel and speak with others, emphasizing love rather than condemnation in proclaiming the Gospel. This is a later spiritual interpretation of his example, distinct from a contemporary record of his travels.

biography: Joseph Chang Song-jip worked in a herb shop in Seoul and was twice widowed. He began studying Catholicism as an adult but stopped when he struggled with its teachings about the Incarnation and Christ's birth. A Catholic friend later persuaded him to resume his religious life.

Joseph turned to prayer, meditation and Scripture, and received baptism and confirmation in 1838. Arrested during the following year's persecution, he explained his beliefs to those urging him to abandon them. After beatings and continued imprisonment, he died in a Seoul prison in May 1839. The Korean bishops include him among their canonized martyrs.

biography: Paola Frassinetti took on household responsibilities in Genoa after her mother's death. Ill health later brought her to her priest brother's parish at Quinto, where conversations with local girls helped reveal a vocation to education. In 1834 she and six companions began a religious community and opened a school for poor children.

The community adopted the work of Saint Dorothy and became the Sisters of Saint Dorothy. Its educational ministry developed despite poverty and practical obstacles, extending from Genoa to Rome and beyond. Paola's approach linked religious formation with access to schooling for those least able to afford it. She was canonized in 1984.

biography: Joseph Mary Tomasi was born into a noble Sicilian family but renounced his inheritance to enter the Theatines. He developed an extensive knowledge of languages and was ordained in Rome in 1673. Liturgy became a central field of study, connecting scholarship with his priestly and religious commitments.

His work included sacramentaries, psalters and chant texts. Later a cardinal, he remained known for learning joined to prayer. His canonization in 1986 recognized a life whose contribution included careful preservation of Christian worship's documentary history.

biography: Paula Montal Fornés lost her father as a child and helped support her family. Growing up in Arenys de Mar, she recognized how limited educational opportunities were for girls. In 1829 she and Inés Busquets opened a school in Figueres, offering a broader education within a Christian setting.

Further schools followed, and cooperation with the Piarists helped shape the Sisters of the Pious Schools. Paula drew on the educational spirituality of Saint Joseph Calasanz and made teaching central to the congregation's religious commitment. Her contribution was not simply founding a school, but building a durable community around girls' education. She was canonized in 2001.

Industrial work was drawing young women into the city, often without adequate support. With Louis Brisson, she helped develop a community responding to the circumstances of these workers.

Her later life included exile in Italy, where she died in 1914. Canonized in 2001, she belonged to a distinct congregation and should not be confused with the Salesian sisters founded in the tradition of John Bosco.

She later served as porter, novice mistress, and superior, giving increasing responsibility to a woman whose admission had initially been reluctant.

In 1890 she and Virgínia Rosa began caring for a woman with cancer, an initiative that grew into the Little Sisters of the Immaculate Conception.

biography: Peter de Betancurt grew up in a poor family in Tenerife and worked as a shepherd before leaving for the Americas. He eventually reached Guatemala, where he worked in textiles. An attempt to prepare for priesthood did not succeed, but it did not end his commitment to Christian service.

A small hospital for convalescents, begun in 1658, became part of the foundation associated with the Bethlehemite community. Canonized in 2002, he offers an example of a substantial vocation outside ordained ministry and of care for those ordinary institutions had overlooked.

biography: José María Rubio Peralta came from a farming family in Dalías and was ordained in 1887. Although he wanted to become a Jesuit, responsibilities that included caring for an elderly priest delayed that step for many years. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1906 after serving in parish and seminary work.

In Madrid he became known for confession, spiritual direction, and straightforward preaching. He also encouraged lay collaborators who organized schools, vocational training, employment assistance, and care for people with illness or disabilities. His contribution included helping others discover how they could serve, not simply carrying out every task himself. He died in 1929 and was canonized in 2003.

With guidance from a priest, she instead served people affected by cholera and gradually discerned a form of community life closely connected to the needs of the city's poor.

She organized accommodation for women attending university, then undertook educational work in Saint Petersburg under restrictions on Catholic religious life. biography: Joseph Freinademetz was born in South Tyrol, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and became a priest in 1875. After parish ministry near home, he joined Arnold Janssen's missionary foundation and left for China in 1879. Preparation in Hong Kong preceded his work in Shandong.

He devoted particular attention to forming local catechists and Chinese priests, including preparing a catechetical manual in Chinese. His ministry involved learning from the people among whom he lived, not simply arriving with a ready-made program. During a typhus outbreak he continued visiting communities and became infected himself. He died in 1908 and was canonized in 2003, alongside Janssen.

biography: Gregory II served as bishop of Rome from 715 to 731. His pontificate unfolded amid disputes over imperial taxation, the government of Italy and the place of sacred images in Christian worship. He resisted attempts by Byzantine imperial authority to determine the Church's teaching about those images.

His life shows how a pope's work could combine a difficult defense of ecclesial independence with encouragement for missionaries and the growth of local churches.

biography: César de Bus was a French priest whose ministry grew out of a decisive change from an unsettled worldly life to prayer, study and service. He was ordained in 1582 and became especially concerned that people without formal education should be able to understand the Christian faith, including those living in rural communities.

He died at Avignon on April 15, 1607, the date of his commemoration, and was canonized in 2022. His legacy concerns accessible religious formation and the sustained work of a teaching community, rather than education reserved for a privileged few.

Her July 16 commemoration is distinct from the July 17 celebration noted in the diocesan proper of Coutances and Avranches.

biography: Jacques Berthieu served as a diocesan priest in France before entering the Jesuits in 1873. He sailed for Madagascar two years later. At Sainte Marie he worked to learn the local language while teaching catechism, visiting Christians and preparing people for the sacraments. He also assisted sick people and supported schooling and agricultural work.

Expulsion orders repeatedly disrupted his ministry and forced him to leave mission stations. He continued serving communities amid conflict rather than abandoning their pastoral needs. In 1896 he was captured and killed after refusing demands that he renounce his faith. His individual canonization recognizes a missionary life that ended in martyrdom. Benedict XVI canonized Jacques Berthieu in 2012.

His later ministry in Lviv combined school catechesis with publishing catechisms and guidance for parents and educators.

He organized charitable institutions and formed a community of women to carry their work forward. The Sisters of Saint Joseph were officially founded in 1884 and served in hospitals, orphanages and other homes, also visiting sick people in their own houses. Prayer and practical assistance remained linked throughout his pastoral and organizational work. Benedict XVI canonized Zygmunt Gorazdowski in 2005.

biography: George Preca grew up in Valletta and Ħamrun and trained in the Malta seminary. Even before his ordination in 1906, he gathered young men for religious instruction. Their meetings developed into the Society of Christian Doctrine, whose lay members received spiritual formation so they could teach others.

A women’s section followed in 1910. The society’s members combined ordinary employment with a disciplined life of prayer and catechesis for children and adults, and regular continuing formation for themselves. Commonly known as M.U.S.E.U.M., the undertaking brought systematic religious teaching into local communities and became the principal institutional expression of Preca’s priestly vocation. Benedict XVI canonized George Preca in 2007.

biography: Artemide Zatti worked as a child laborer in Italy before his family emigrated to Argentina because of poverty. At Bahía Blanca he worked in a hotel and a brick factory and encountered the Salesians through parish life. He sought to join them but contracted tuberculosis while caring for a sick priest and moved to Viedma.

After recovering, he became a Salesian lay brother and devoted himself to the hospital there. He qualified to dispense medicines and later assumed administrative responsibilities while nursing patients. His care also extended beyond the hospital through visits around Viedma and nearby Patagones, often carrying medicines by bicycle to those unable to reach him. Francis canonized Artemide Zatti in 2022.

After ordination in 1571 he developed catechetical instruction for children that the bishop extended to churches throughout the city.

Opposition to his reforming work led to banishment from Lucca while he was visiting Rome. There he continued catechesis and undertook responsibilities in the reform of religious houses and the preparation of missionary work. Pius XI canonized John Leonardi in 1938.

Religious persecution closed a newspaper he had founded and forced him to travel without a permanent home, sometimes using disguises so he could visit sick people and administer the sacraments.

His episcopal ministry remained closely concerned with seminary formation and pastoral service under conditions of exile and clandestine activity. Benedict XVI canonized Rafael Guízar Valencia in 2006.

biography: Leonard Murialdo grew up in Turin and studied with the Piarists at Savona. A period of spiritual difficulty brought him home, where renewed religious commitment eventually led to the priesthood. Ordained in 1851, he taught catechism in an oratory and, with John Bosco’s encouragement, became director of the Saint Louis oratory.

In 1873 he founded the Congregation of Saint Joseph to serve young people, especially those who were poor or abandoned, giving an enduring community structure to his educational and charitable initiatives. Paul VI canonized Leonard Murialdo in 1970.

biography: José Gregorio Hernández Cisneros grew up in Isnotú and studied in Caracas, eventually qualifying as a physician. In 1889 he was sent to Paris for advanced work in microbiology, bacteriology, histology and experimental physiology. On returning to Venezuela he helped introduce these subjects into university teaching.

He combined his academic career and medical practice with a committed Catholic life and membership in the Franciscan Third Order. He gave particular attention to poor patients, charging them nothing and sometimes supplying money for medicines. This practical service brought him recognition as a physician of the poor while he continued contributing to medical education. Leo XIV canonized José Gregorio Hernández Cisneros in 2025.
